The existing global `blog` to `Poon Report` and `it's an STD` to an editorial explanation suggestions are unsafe. The blog is resolved only beside its URL; jokes remain literal with metadata corrections.

CDC identifies chlamydia as a common bacterial STI that is often asymptomatic but can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy and infertility. It is treatable, not harmless, and partners and retesting matter: https://www.cdc.gov/chlamydia/about/index.html and https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/chlamydia.htm

CDC guidance no longer supports calling hepatitis C inevitably permanent; current direct-acting antiviral treatment cures most people. Sexual transmission risk varies by context: https://www.cdc.gov/hepatitis-c/treatment/index.html and https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/hcv.htm

SAMHSA says hallucinogens including LSD can change perception and sense of reality and cause hallucinations, confusion, fear, panic and risky behavior. Steve Lee's visions are evidence of a frightening intoxication experience, not proof of demons, reptilians or other dimensions: https://www.samhsa.gov/substance-use/learn/hallucinogens

Donohue and Levitt's 2001 abortion/crime paper and 2019 update argue for a causal reduction, while Ted Joyce's NBER studies find little causal support and challenge robustness. The archive labels this a contested hypothesis, not settled fact or a basis for predicting any child: https://www.nber.org/papers/w8004, https://www.nber.org/papers/w25863, https://www.nber.org/papers/w8319 and https://www.nber.org/papers/w12607

The official Afghan Premier League sources reviewed for Episode 094 confirm a real league but not the private purchase/coaching plan. Showing Steve a website does not promote the prior improvisation into project history.

summary: Episode 095 clarifies DVDASA's production method more directly than the prior episode: arguments and conversations are not prewritten radio bits, but recurring segments are deliberately attempted and often displaced by whatever develops in the room. The revived Ask Asa segment contains a useful first-person distinction between performance and emotional detachment. Asa describes cameras and crews as part of the fantasy, acknowledges that real feelings can arise during a scene, and says those feelings often fade when ordinary life resumes. That account is retained as one performer's experience, not generalized to an industry. A body-transformation proposal raises a real creative conflict—ambition, bodily autonomy, health and a spouse's boundaries—but the conversation repeatedly degrades into racial, transphobic and explicit spectacle; the archive does not repackage it as a serious art project. The abortion discussion correctly centers that people can make difficult reproductive decisions for their own lives, but two anecdotes cannot prove abortion causes professional success. The crime-drop claim is a contested economic hypothesis, not settled causal fact and never a warrant to label an unwanted child a future criminal. Chlamydia is bacterial, commonly asymptomatic and treatable but potentially serious; hepatitis C is now usually curable; herpes and gonorrhea are not dismissed as inconsequential. The closing Trippin' with Steve Lee story is the strongest new material. Steve narrates an LSD experience at Arizona State, a friend's dangerous crisis and his own frightening visual hallucinations. He later identifies the experience as part of why he got sober. His supernatural interpretation is preserved as belief, while current drug guidance explains that LSD alters perception and sense of reality and can cause panic, confusion and hazardous behavior. The account does not verify demons, reptilians or dimensions. Twenty restricted spans protect listener handles, private partners, reproductive and STI histories, sex workers, residences, medical details, explicit instruction, coercive hypotheticals, drug history and identifiable bystanders. Named dialogue remains withheld.
